items.text: This is a dedicated deep dive into the data scientist path specifically, not a general machine learning guide.

blocks.heading: Statistics and Probability, the Real Foundation

items.text: This is the layer most beginner roadmaps rush through to get to the "fun" part.

Mean, median, variance, and standard deviation sound basic, but knowing when a distribution is skewed, when an average is hiding two very different groups, and when a metric is being gamed is what separates useful analysis from a dashboard nobody trusts.
Practise on messy, real business data, not clean textbook datasets.
This is the single most under-taught skill in beginner data science content, and it is one of the most reliably tested skills in real interviews at product-led companies.
This framing step is where most self-taught learners skip straight to running numbers.
Stopping a test early because the result looks good is one of the most common ways teams fool themselves.
Sequence decides whether this roadmap actually works.
Start here, not with Python or machine learning.
Work through distributions, sampling, and hypothesis testing using a real or realistic dataset, not through formulas in isolation.

blocks.heading: Portfolio Built on Insight, Not Deployment

items.text: This is where the data scientist path and the machine learning engineer path diverge most visibly in practice.

Take a real or public dataset, frame a business question (did a pricing change actually increase revenue, or did an intervention actually reduce churn), and show your full reasoning from hypothesis to conclusion, including what could confound the result.
Design and simulate or analyse an experiment: state the hypothesis, the metric, the sample size logic, and the honest interpretation of the result, including any guardrail metric that moved.
Predictive modelling is the most exciting part of the roadmap and the least useful place to start.
A technically excellent analysis that nobody can act on because it was buried in jargon or a 40-slide deck does not move a business decision.
Deploying a model with Docker and an API is a genuinely valuable skill, but it answers the wrong question for most data scientist interviews.
There is no single honest week count here, and any roadmap that hands you an exact number is guessing.

People who already sit close to this work, statistics or economics graduates, existing business analysts, or anyone already comfortable in SQL, often reach an interview-ready portfolio in a focused stretch of a few months.
The competition here is not single-stage, and it is worth naming both stages separately.
Do not open another statistics course before you have picked your first analysis question and started pulling data for it with SQL.
Start with SQL and one real dataset, before any statistics theory or machine learning model.
Pick one business question you can defend end to end, and build the full analysis before you start a second one.

blocks.heading: Science From Another Field: the Switcher Route
rows: Commerce, finance or accounts
You already read numbers and know how businesses measure money.
An SQL and Excel analysis of a public financial or sales dataset, with a clear recommendation.
Collecting machine-learning certificates before you can explain a basic result.
Engineering (any branch)
Comfort with maths, code and structured problem-solving.
One analysis tied to your own branch's data, such as sensor, process or energy data.
Jumping to model tuning and skipping statistics and SQL.
Arts, humanities or science
Research habits, writing and domain depth in a subject.
A short, well-written analysis of a question from your subject, using open data.
Assuming maths is a wall. Applied statistics is learnable and checkable.
Working professional in operations, marketing, HR or sales
You know which decisions matter and where the data is messy.
A small analysis of a real problem in your own workplace, with permission and without confidential data.
Quitting your job to study. Switch inside your company first, if it is possible.

blocks.heading: SQL and Data Wrangling, Before Python Models

items.text: Joins and aggregations: pulling data across multiple tables is the daily reality of the job, not an occasional task.
Window functions: running totals, rank-within-group, and period-over-period comparisons are the queries that turn raw rows into an actual business answer.
Data cleaning inside SQL: deduplication, handling nulls, and catching inconsistent formats before the data ever reaches Python saves hours later and catches errors that pandas alone will not flag.
Query performance basics: knowing why a query is slow and how indexing and filtering order affect it matters once you work with real production-sized tables instead of a sample CSV.
